q.s: A 38-year-old man vomited repeatedly after a night of binge drinking. On the last few episodes he vomited bright red blood. He is now comfortable. Pulse is 92/min and blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. There is no crepitus or chest pain. Hemoglobin is 13.6 g/dL. Endoscopy shows a longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction.
e: Wrong. A large submucosal artery, not a tear.
Correct. Partial-thickness, longitudinal laceration at the GE junction from severe vomiting; painless hematemesis, usually self-limited.
Wrong. Dilated submucosal veins in cirrhosis.
cl: vomited repeatedly after a night of binge drinking
Alcohol and severe vomiting are classic triggers.
There is no crepitus or chest pain
longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction
q.ch: Binge drinking + retching → hematemesis + GE junction mucosal tear, no mediastinitis → Mallory-Weiss.
q.tr: Mallory-Weiss = mucosa; Boerhaave = burst through all layers.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large amount of bright red blood. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg. He has spider angiomas, palmar erythema and splenomegaly. Two large-bore IV lines are placed and blood transfusion is started.
e: Wrong. Does not stop variceal bleeding.
Correct. A somatostatin analog that inhibits splanchnic vasodilatory hormones and reduces portal pressure in acute variceal bleeding.
Wrong. Prevents encephalopathy, does not stop bleeding.
Wrong. Does not lower portal pressure.
Wrong. Nonselective β-blockers are used for prophylaxis, not active bleeding with shock.
cl: spider angiomas, palmar erythema and splenomegaly
Stigmata of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension.
vomits a large amount of bright red blood
Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg
q.ch: Cirrhosis + massive hematemesis + portal hypertension → variceal bleed → octreotide + endoscopic banding.
q.tr: Octreotide treats bleeds; propranolol prevents them.
q.q2: Which drug should be started to reduce portal blood flow while awaiting endoscopy?

q.s: A 45-year-old woman has episodes of severe chest pain that occur while eating and sometimes wake her at night. She has intermittent dysphagia for both solids and liquids. Cardiac stress testing is normal. A barium swallow shows a "corkscrew" esophagus. Esophageal manometry is shown.
e: Correct. Simultaneous, uncoordinated, high-amplitude contractions instead of a peristaltic wave cause chest pain and a corkscrew esophagus.
Wrong. Nonrelaxing LES with bird's beak.
cl: severe chest pain that occur while eating
dysphagia for both solids and liquids
q.ch: Chest pain with swallowing + normal cardiac workup + corkscrew esophagus + simultaneous high-pressure contractions (figure) → distal esophageal spasm.
q.tr: Normal peristalsis is sequential (staggered peaks); spasm fires all levels at once.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
q.fc: Esophageal body pressures after a swallow

q.s: A 72-year-old man has bad breath, a gurgling sound in his neck when he swallows and regurgitation of food he ate days earlier. He has had several episodes of aspiration pneumonia. Barium swallow shows a pouch arising posteriorly just above the upper esophageal sphincter.
o: True diverticulum of the midesophagus from traction
False diverticulum through the Killian triangle
e: Wrong. Midesophageal traction diverticula involve all layers.
Wrong. A membrane, not a pouch.
Correct. Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal false (pulsion) diverticulum herniating through the Killian triangle above the cricopharyngeus.
cl: regurgitation of food he ate days earlier
just above the upper esophageal sphincter
q.ch: Elderly + halitosis + gurgling + regurgitation of old food + posterior pouch above the UES → Zenker → false diverticulum through Killian triangle.
q.tr: Zenker = False (only mucosa and submucosa); Meckel = True (all layers).
q.q2: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

q.s: A 49-year-old woman has heartburn and difficulty swallowing. She has thickened, tight skin on her fingers and face, color changes of her fingers in the cold and small dilated vessels on her face. Esophageal manometry shows absent peristalsis in the distal esophagus and very low LES pressure.
o: Atrophy and fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle
e: Wrong. Polymyositis affects the upper (skeletal muscle) esophagus.
Correct. Scleroderma (CREST) causes smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis, low LES pressure, poor peristalsis and reflux.
cl: thickened, tight skin on her fingers and face
color changes of her fingers in the cold
small dilated vessels on her face
q.ch: CREST features + reflux + absent distal peristalsis + low LES pressure → scleroderma → smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis.
q.tr: Achalasia: LES too tight. Scleroderma: LES too loose.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her esophageal findings?

q.s: A 64-year-old man from Japan has early satiety, epigastric pain and a 9-kg weight loss. Examination shows a hard, enlarged lymph node above the left clavicle. Endoscopy shows a thickened, rigid stomach wall without a discrete mass. Biopsy shows cells with mucin pushing the nucleus to the side.
e: Wrong. Usually a discrete ulcerated mass.
Correct. Signet ring cells infiltrating the wall cause linitis plastica; spread to the Virchow node.
Wrong. Lymphocytes, not signet ring cells.
cl: hard, enlarged lymph node above the left clavicle
mucin pushing the nucleus to the side
q.ch: Weight loss + early satiety + Virchow node + rigid stomach + signet ring cells → diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma.
q.tr: Diffuse type: signet rings and leather bottle; spreads to Virchow, Sister Mary Joseph and Krukenberg.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 30-year-old man is admitted with second- and third-degree burns over 45% of his body surface area. On day 4 he has hematemesis and a falling hemoglobin. Endoscopy shows multiple shallow erosions in the stomach and duodenum.
o: Increased vagal stimulation and acid production
e: Wrong. Cushing ulcer after brain injury.
Correct. Curling ulcer: acute gastritis after burns from hypovolemia and decreased mucosal blood flow.
cl: burns over 45% of his body surface area
q.ch: Severe burns → hypovolemia → mucosal ischemia → acute erosive gastritis (Curling ulcer).
q.tr: "Burned by the Curling iron"; "Always Cushion the brain."
q.q2: Which of the following is the mechanism of his lesions?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has fatigue, tingling in her feet and loss of position sense. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL with an MCV of 118 fL. Serum gastrin is markedly elevated. Antibodies to intrinsic factor are present.
e: Correct. Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells in the body and fundus, causing achlorhydria, high gastrin and B12 deficiency.
Wrong. H. pylori gastritis mainly affects the antrum.
cl: Dorsal column involvement from B12 deficiency.
q.ch: Autoimmune disease + megaloblastic anemia + neuropathy + high gastrin + anti-IF → autoimmune gastritis → parietal cells in body/fundus.
q.tr: Type A (Autoimmune) = body; type B (Bacterial) = antrum.
q.q2: Which region of the stomach is most affected?

q.s: A 67-year-old woman with osteoarthritis takes naproxen several times a day. She has had burning epigastric pain for 2 months that becomes worse soon after meals, and she has lost weight because she is afraid to eat. H. pylori testing is negative.
o: Decreased prostaglandin synthesis reducing mucosal protection
e: Correct. NSAIDs inhibit COX and reduce prostaglandins, decreasing mucus and bicarbonate and causing gastric ulcers.
cl: takes naproxen several times a day
q.ch: Chronic NSAID use + pain worse with meals + weight loss → gastric ulcer → reduced prostaglandin-mediated protection.
q.tr: Gastric ulcer: pain Greater with meals; Duodenal ulcer: Decreases with meals.
q.q2: Which mechanism best explains her condition?

q.s: A 46-year-old woman had a partial gastrectomy 3 months ago. About 20 minutes after meals she has cramping, diarrhea, sweating, palpitations and lightheadedness. About 2 hours after meals she becomes shaky and confused. Her plasma glucose after a meal is shown.
o: Excess insulin release after rapid glucose absorption
e: Wrong. A late complication, but not this.
Wrong. Bloating and diarrhea, not hypoglycemia.
Correct. Dumping syndrome: hyperosmolar food enters the small bowel quickly (early fluid shift symptoms); the glucose spike causes excessive insulin and late hypoglycemia.
cl: Loss of pyloric control of emptying.
q.ch: Gastric surgery → rapid emptying of hyperosmolar food → early fluid shifts + glucose spike then excess insulin → late hypoglycemia (figure).
q.tr: Early dumping = fluid shift; late dumping = insulin overshoot.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her late symptoms?

q.s: A 35-year-old man returned 6 months ago from a 2-year stay in rural India. He has chronic diarrhea, weight loss and fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Stool studies for ova and parasites are negative. Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative. Small bowel biopsy shows villous blunting throughout the small intestine.
e: Correct. Tropical sprue responds to antibiotics and folate.
cl: Unlike celiac, which is mainly proximal.
q.ch: Tropics + malabsorption + megaloblastic anemia + negative celiac serology → tropical sprue → antibiotics and folate.
q.tr: Tropical sprue = celiac-like biopsy + travel history + negative serology.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 28-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis has 12 bloody bowel movements daily. She now has fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension and tenderness. Abdominal x-ray shows a transverse colon diameter of 8 cm. She recently started loperamide.
e: Correct. Toxic megacolon can perforate; avoid antimotility drugs and treat urgently.
cl: Antimotility drugs can precipitate toxic megacolon.
q.ch: Severe UC + systemic toxicity + colon >6 cm (antimotility drug) → toxic megacolon → perforation risk.
q.tr: Never give antimotility drugs in severe colitis.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most serious immediate risk of her condition?

q.s: A 64-year-old woman has had watery, nonbloody diarrhea 6 to 8 times a day for 4 months. She takes sertraline and omeprazole. Colonoscopy shows normal-appearing mucosa. Biopsy shows a thickened subepithelial collagen band.
e: Correct. Chronic watery diarrhea in older women with normal-appearing mucosa; collagenous or lymphocytic subtypes on biopsy.
q.ch: Older woman + chronic watery diarrhea + PPI/SSRI + normal colonoscopy + collagen band → microscopic colitis.
q.tr: Microscopic colitis: "it looks normal until you look under the microscope."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 19-year-old man has had pain for 18 hours that began around the umbilicus and moved to the right lower quadrant. He has nausea and anorexia. Temperature is 38.1°C. Pressing on the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant. White blood cell count is 14,200/mm³.
e: Wrong. Diaphragmatic referral to the shoulder.
Correct. Midgut visceral pain is referred to the umbilicus (T10); once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed, pain localizes to McBurney point.
cl: moved to the right lower quadrant
Pressing on the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant
q.ch: Periumbilical pain migrating to the RLQ + fever + Rovsing sign → appendicitis; visceral pain referred to T10.
q.tr: Appendix pain starts at the belly button (T10) and settles at McBurney point.
q.q2: The initial periumbilical pain is carried by visceral afferent fibers entering the spinal cord at which level?

q.s: A newborn girl has bilious vomiting within hours of her first feed. She has a flat facial profile, upslanting eyes and a single palmar crease. Her mother had polyhydramnios. Abdominal x-ray shows two large gas bubbles in the upper abdomen with no distal bowel gas.
o: Failure of the duodenal lumen to recanalize
e: Correct. Duodenal atresia: "double bubble," associated with Down syndrome.
cl: bilious vomiting within hours of her first feed
flat facial profile, upslanting eyes and a single palmar crease
Fetus cannot swallow and absorb amniotic fluid.
q.ch: Neonate + bilious vomiting + Down syndrome + polyhydramnios + double bubble → duodenal atresia → failed recanalization.
q.tr: Duodenal atresia = failed recanalization; jejunal/ileal atresia = vascular accident.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains this condition?

q.s: A newborn boy has bowel protruding through a defect to the right of a normal umbilical cord. The bowel is not covered by a membrane. His mother is 19 years old and smoked during pregnancy.
o: It results from failure of lateral fold closure and is usually not associated with chromosomal abnormalities
It is caused by failure of neural crest migration
It is a defect of the diaphragm
It is covered by peritoneum and is often associated with trisomies
It results from persistent herniation of midgut through the umbilical ring
e: Correct. Gastroschisis: uncovered bowel lateral to the umbilicus, associated with young maternal age and smoking.
cl: to the right of a normal umbilical cord
19 years old and smoked during pregnancy
q.ch: Uncovered bowel beside a normal cord + young, smoking mother → gastroschisis → lateral fold closure failure.
q.tr: Gastroschisis = "extrudes" uncovered; omphalocele = "sealed" in peritoneum.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes this defect compared with the alternative diagnosis?

q.s: A 3-week-old girl suddenly develops bilious vomiting and is irritable. She was feeding well before. The abdomen is mildly distended. Upper GI contrast study shows the duodenojejunal junction to the right of the midline with a "corkscrew" appearance of the proximal small bowel.
e: Correct. Abnormal rotation leaves the bowel on a narrow mesentery prone to midgut volvulus; Ladd bands may also obstruct.
Wrong. Duodenal narrowing without a corkscrew.
cl: Bilious vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency.
to the right of the midline
q.ch: Infant + new bilious vomiting + malpositioned DJ junction + corkscrew → malrotation with midgut volvulus.
q.tr: Bilious vomiting in an infant = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely underlying anomaly?

q.s: A boy born at 28 weeks' gestation is fed formula in the neonatal intensive care unit. On day 10 he develops feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and bloody stools. Abdominal x-ray shows bubbly gas within the bowel wall.
e: Correct. Premature, formula-fed infants develop intestinal necrosis, usually in the terminal ileum and proximal colon, with pneumatosis intestinalis.
cl: Formula feeding is a risk factor.
bubbly gas within the bowel wall
q.ch: Premature + formula-fed + distension + bloody stools + pneumatosis → NEC.
q.tr: Pneumatosis in a preemie = NEC.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 67-year-old man is admitted with fever. Blood cultures grow a gram-positive coccus that is nonhemolytic, grows in bile and hydrolyzes esculin, but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl. Echocardiography shows a vegetation on the aortic valve. He has mild iron deficiency anemia.
e: Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (S. bovis) bacteremia or endocarditis is associated with colorectal cancer.
cl: grows in bile and hydrolyzes esculin, but does not grow in 6.5% NaCl
q.ch: S. gallolyticus endocarditis + iron deficiency → colorectal cancer → colonoscopy.
q.tr: S. bovis in the blood → look in the colon.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?

q.s: A 71-year-old woman had an episode of hypotension during cardiac bypass surgery yesterday. Today she has crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea. Colonoscopy shows edematous, ulcerated mucosa at the splenic flexure with a sharp transition to normal mucosa.
o: It is drained by the portal vein only
It has the highest bacterial load
It is supplied only by the celiac trunk
It is a watershed area between the SMA and IMA territories
e: Correct. Colonic ischemia commonly occurs at watershed areas: the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid junction.
cl: crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea
q.ch: Hypotension → low flow to watershed areas → splenic flexure ischemia → crampy pain then hematochezia.
q.tr: Splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and rectosigmoid (IMA/hypogastric) are watershed zones.
q.q2: Why is this region especially vulnerable?

q.s: A 68-year-old thin woman has a tender, irreducible bulge in her right groin below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the pubic tubercle. She has vomiting and abdominal distension.
e: Wrong. Direct hernia, above the ligament.
Correct. Femoral hernias pass below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, medial to the femoral vein; more common in women and prone to incarceration.
q.ch: Woman + groin bulge below the inguinal ligament + incarceration → femoral hernia through the femoral canal.
q.tr: Femoral: below the ligament, medial to the femoral vein ("NAVEL": nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics).
q.q2: Through which structure does this hernia pass?

q.s: A 70-year-old man has a bulge in his left groin that appears when he stands and strains. It does not enter the scrotum. At surgery, the hernia sac lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
o: It passes through the deep inguinal ring
It protrudes through Hesselbach triangle and is covered only by the external spermatic fascia
It is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
It passes below the inguinal ligament
It occurs most often in infants
It results from a patent processus vaginalis
e: Correct. Direct inguinal hernia: medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through a weak transversalis fascia, common in older men.
cl: Direct hernias rarely reach the scrotum.
medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
q.ch: Older man + groin bulge medial to the inferior epigastric vessels → direct hernia through Hesselbach triangle.
q.tr: "MDs don't LIe": Medial = Direct, Lateral = Indirect.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes this hernia?

q.s: A 46-year-old man who drinks a pint of vodka daily has fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. The liver is enlarged and tender. His test results are shown.
o: Councilman bodies from viral injury alone
Swollen, necrotic hepatocytes with Mallory bodies and neutrophils
e: Correct. Alcohol-associated hepatitis: ballooning, Mallory bodies (damaged keratin) and neutrophil infiltration; AST:ALT ratio >2.
cl: drinks a pint of vodka daily
fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice
The liver is enlarged and tender
q.ch: Heavy drinking + fever, RUQ pain, jaundice + AST:ALT >2 with AST <500, high GGT, macrocytosis (table) → alcohol-associated hepatitis → Mallory bodies.
q.tr: "Make a toAST with alcohol": AST > ALT (ratio > 2).
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on liver biopsy?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes and hypertriglyceridemia has mildly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 82 U/L, AST 54 U/L). She drinks alcohol only on special occasions. Hepatitis serologies are negative. Ultrasound shows a bright, echogenic liver.
e: Wrong. Minimal alcohol use; AST:ALT would be >2.
Correct. MASLD: fatty infiltration associated with metabolic syndrome; ALT > AST.
cl: drinks alcohol only on special occasions
q.ch: Metabolic syndrome + ALT > AST + minimal alcohol + echogenic liver → MASLD.
q.tr: ALT > AST: "lipids" (MASLD); AST > ALT: alcohol.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 32-year-old woman who has taken oral contraceptive pills for 12 years has sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg. CT shows a 7-cm solitary liver mass with hemorrhage and free intraperitoneal blood. α-Fetoprotein is normal.
e: Correct. Benign tumor linked to oral contraceptives and anabolic steroids; can rupture and bleed.
Wrong. Biopsy risk, but rarely ruptures spontaneously.
cl: sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and lightheadedness
q.ch: Young woman on OCPs + solitary liver mass + rupture with hemoperitoneum → hepatic adenoma.
q.tr: OCPs + liver mass that bleeds = hepatic adenoma.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 40-year-old woman has a 3-cm liver mass found incidentally on ultrasound for gallbladder evaluation. She is asymptomatic and liver enzymes are normal. Contrast CT shows peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in toward the center on delayed images.
e: Wrong. Not needed for an asymptomatic lesion.
Wrong. Contraindicated because of hemorrhage risk.
Correct. Cavernous hemangioma, the most common benign liver tumor; biopsy is contraindicated and asymptomatic lesions need no treatment.
cl: peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in toward the center
q.ch: Incidental liver mass + peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill → hemangioma → no biopsy, observe.
q.tr: Never biopsy a hemangioma.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 22-year-old college student notices that the whites of his eyes turn yellow during exam week, when he skips meals, and during colds. Examination is otherwise normal. Results before and after a 48-hour fast are shown.
e: Correct. Gilbert syndrome: mildly reduced UGT activity; benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with stress, fasting or illness.
Wrong. Used in Crigler-Najjar type II.
cl: during exam week, when he skips meals, and during colds
Stress, fasting and illness trigger jaundice.
whites of his eyes turn yellow
Scleral icterus appears at bilirubin around 2–3 mg/dL.
q.ch: Intermittent jaundice with fasting/stress + isolated unconjugated rise + no hemolysis, normal enzymes (table) → Gilbert → reassurance.
q.tr: Gilbert: unconjugated bilirubin rises with fasting; no hemolysis; no treatment.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 44-year-old woman with obesity has had constant right upper quadrant pain for 10 hours after a fatty meal, radiating to the right shoulder. Temperature is 38.3°C. She stops inhaling during deep palpation under the right costal margin. Bilirubin is normal. Results of a cholescintigraphy (HIDA) scan are shown.
e: Correct. Acute cholecystitis: a stone blocks the cystic duct, so the gallbladder never fills.
Wrong. The liver takes up tracer.
cl: constant right upper quadrant pain for 10 hours after a fatty meal
Persistent pain beyond simple biliary colic.
Referred pain via the phrenic nerve.
The common bile duct is not obstructed.
q.ch: Fatty meal + prolonged RUQ pain + fever + Murphy sign + gallbladder never fills on HIDA (table) → cystic duct obstruction → acute cholecystitis.
q.tr: HIDA: no gallbladder = cystic duct blocked; no duodenum = CBD blocked.
q.q2: What is the most likely cause of the scan findings?

q.s: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing gallstones has an abdominal CT for back pain. It shows a gallbladder with a continuous rim of calcium in its wall. She has no abdominal symptoms.
e: Correct. Porcelain gallbladder (calcified wall from chronic cholecystitis) is associated with gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
cl: continuous rim of calcium in its wall
q.ch: Chronic gallstones → chronic cholecystitis → calcified wall (porcelain gallbladder) → cancer risk → cholecystectomy.
q.tr: Porcelain gallbladder → think gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

q.s: A 50-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 25 years has chronic epigastric pain radiating to the back, bulky foul-smelling stools that float, and weight loss. He was recently diagnosed with diabetes. His test results are shown.
o: Vitamin A, D, E and K
e: Wrong. Alcohol-related, but not from pancreatic insufficiency.
Correct. Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency causes fat malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.
cl: Most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in adults.
epigastric pain radiating to the back
q.ch: Alcohol + chronic pain + steatorrhea + diabetes + calcifications, low fecal elastase, normal lipase (table) → chronic pancreatitis → fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
q.tr: In chronic pancreatitis, lipase may be normal; the pancreas has burned out.
q.q2: Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely to develop?

q.s: A 45-year-old man had acute alcohol-related pancreatitis 5 weeks ago. He now has early satiety, persistent epigastric fullness and a palpable epigastric mass. Serum lipase remains elevated. CT shows a round, fluid-filled collection next to the pancreas with a thick wall.
o: Granulation tissue without an epithelial lining
e: Wrong. True cysts or neoplastic cysts.
Correct. Pancreatic pseudocyst: a fluid collection lined by granulation tissue, not epithelium.
cl: fluid-filled collection next to the pancreas with a thick wall
q.ch: Pancreatitis weeks ago + persistent lipase + walled peripancreatic fluid → pseudocyst → granulation tissue wall.
q.tr: Pseudo-cyst = no real epithelial lining.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes the wall of this lesion?

q.s: A 2-day-old boy has nonbilious and bilious vomiting after feeds. Imaging shows narrowing of the second part of the duodenum. At surgery, a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the duodenum.
o: Abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud, which encircles the duodenum
Failure of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts to fuse
e: Correct. Annular pancreas: the ventral bud (sometimes bifid) wraps around the second part of the duodenum.
cl: narrowing of the second part of the duodenum
ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the duodenum
Obstruction near or distal to the ampulla.
q.ch: Neonatal duodenal obstruction + ring of pancreas around D2 → annular pancreas → abnormal ventral bud rotation.
q.tr: Annular = ventral bud encircles; divisum = buds fail to fuse.
q.q2: Which embryologic error caused this condition?

q.s: A 34-year-old woman has had three episodes of acute pancreatitis. She does not drink alcohol, has normal triglycerides and calcium, and has no gallstones. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography shows most pancreatic drainage through the minor papilla.
e: Wrong. Pancreatic tissue in another site.
Correct. Failure of fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts; most drainage via the minor papilla; may cause recurrent pancreatitis.
cl: does not drink alcohol, has normal triglycerides and calcium, and has no gallstones
most pancreatic drainage through the minor papilla
q.ch: Recurrent idiopathic pancreatitis + drainage through the minor papilla → pancreas divisum.
q.tr: Divisum = ducts "divided," never fused.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely underlying anomaly?

q.s: A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis has dilated, tortuous veins radiating from his umbilicus. He also has hemorrhoids and splenomegaly.
e: Correct. Caput medusae: portosystemic anastomosis between paraumbilical (portal) veins and small epigastric (systemic) veins.
cl: dilated, tortuous veins radiating from his umbilicus
q.ch: Cirrhosis → portal hypertension → paraumbilical-to-epigastric shunting → caput medusae.
q.tr: Gut, butt and caput: esophagus (left gastric), rectum (superior rectal), umbilicus (paraumbilical).
q.q2: The umbilical veins connect the systemic circulation with which portal vein tributary?

q.s: A 70-year-old woman who had a gastric bypass operation 4 years ago has bloating, chronic diarrhea and weight loss. She takes omeprazole daily. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 110 fL. Serum folate is elevated. A glucose breath test shows an early rise in hydrogen.
e: Correct. Anatomic changes and achlorhydria (PPI) promote SIBO; bacteria consume B12 and produce folate.
Wrong. Not with high folate and early breath rise.
q.ch: Altered anatomy + PPI + diarrhea + B12 deficiency with high folate + early breath H2 rise → SIBO.
q.tr: SIBO: low B12, high folate.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 61-year-old woman has increasing abdominal girth and weight loss. She has no history of liver disease and no stigmata of cirrhosis. Ascitic fluid analysis is shown.
e: Correct. SAAG = 3.5 − 2.8 = 0.7 (<1.1) indicates a nonportal cause; malignant cells confirm carcinomatosis (e.g., ovarian cancer).
cl: no history of liver disease and no stigmata of cirrhosis
increasing abdominal girth and weight loss
Ovarian cancer is a classic source of carcinomatosis.
q.ch: SAAG 0.7 (<1.1) + high protein + malignant cytology (table) → nonportal ascites → peritoneal carcinomatosis.
q.tr: SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension; <1.1 = peritoneum is the problem (cancer, TB, pancreatitis, nephrotic).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her ascites?

q.s: A 47-year-old woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes has nausea, early satiety and vomiting of undigested food hours after meals. A gastric emptying study is delayed. She is started on a drug that also increases LES tone. Two weeks later she develops restlessness and an inability to sit still.
e: Correct. Metoclopramide is a D2 antagonist that increases gastric emptying and LES tone; it can cause akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia.
Wrong. Erythromycin is a motilin agonist.
cl: vomiting of undigested food hours after meals
q.ch: Diabetic gastroparesis → prokinetic that raises LES tone → akathisia → D2 antagonist (metoclopramide).
q.tr: Metoclopramide: prokinetic plus antipsychotic-type side effects.
q.q2: Which receptor does this drug block?

q.s: A 26-year-old man with ulcerative colitis is treated with a drug that is split by colonic bacteria into an antibacterial and an anti-inflammatory component. A year later, he and his wife are evaluated for infertility. His semen analysis shows a low sperm count.
o: Switch to mesalamine and repeat semen analysis later
Continue the drug; the finding is unrelated
e: Correct. Sulfasalazine (sulfapyridine + 5-ASA) causes reversible oligospermia; switching to mesalamine allows recovery.
cl: split by colonic bacteria into an antibacterial and an anti-inflammatory component
q.ch: UC on sulfasalazine + oligospermia → reversible drug effect → switch to mesalamine.
q.tr: Sulfasalazine's sulfapyridine causes most of its adverse effects, including oligospermia.

q.s: A 72-year-old woman has taken omeprazole for 8 years. She now has muscle cramps, tremor and fatigue. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. Serum calcium is 7.8 mg/dL and potassium is 3.1 mEq/L despite supplements. PTH is inappropriately low.
e: Correct. Long-term PPI use causes hypomagnesemia, which impairs PTH secretion and causes refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia.
cl: Refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia suggest low magnesium.
Magnesium is needed for PTH secretion.
q.ch: Long-term PPI → hypomagnesemia → impaired PTH release and renal K+ wasting → refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia.
q.tr: Refractory hypokalemia or hypocalcemia? Check magnesium.
q.q2: Which electrolyte disorder most likely underlies her findings?

q.s: A 41-year-old woman with obesity starts a weight-loss drug. She develops oily spotting, flatulence with discharge and urgent bowel movements, especially after fatty meals. Months later she reports poor night vision.
o: Inhibition of gastric and pancreatic lipase
e: Wrong. Acarbose causes flatulence but not steatorrhea.
Correct. Orlistat reduces fat absorption, causing steatorrhea and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.
cl: oily spotting, flatulence with discharge and urgent bowel movements
q.ch: Weight-loss drug + steatorrhea + vitamin A deficiency → lipase inhibitor (orlistat).
q.tr: Orlistat: fat goes out, and fat-soluble vitamins go with it.
